p: The KJV has "called his twelve disciples together," following the Textus Receptus.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort and the Byzantine text (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Textus Receptus (KJV "his twelve disciples")
readings.orig: συγκαλεσάμενος δὲ τοὺς δώδεκα μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: having called together his twelve disciples

why: Even the Byzantine text has only "the Twelve." The longer form explains who the Twelve are, as Matthew 10:1 does; it changes nothing in the meaning.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV have "staves," plural, as in the Byzantine text of Matthew 10:10.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "neither staves")

why: The plural softens the clash with Mark 6:8, which allows one staff: if the ban is on "staffs," a single walking stick might seem allowed. The singular is the harder reading and is printed by all the critical editions, so the plural is probably a scribe's harmonizing.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "by him": Herod heard of "all that was done by him."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "all that was done by him")
readings.en: all the things done by him
readings.plain: everything that was being done by him

why: The added words make plain that Herod heard about Jesus. In the shorter text Herod hears of everything happening, the Twelve's mission included (9:6). The addition reads like a clarification, as in Mark 6:14.

p: The oldest text says "to a town called Bethsaida." The KJV has "into a desert place belonging to the city called Bethsaida."

readings.w: P75 (about 175–225), Codex Sinaiticus as corrected (300s), Vaticanus (300s), L, 33 and the Coptic versions (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Codex Alexandrinus (400s), C (400s), W (400s) and the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: εἰς τόπον ἔρημον πόλεως καλουμένης Βηθσαϊδάν
readings.en: to a deserted place of a town called Bethsaida
readings.plain: to a lonely spot near a town called Bethsaida

why: Metzger reports several readings here: "to a deserted place" (the first hand of Sinaiticus and the Old Syriac), "to a village called Bethsaida" (Codex Bezae, 400s), and the Byzantine text combining place and town. The simple "to a town called Bethsaida" best explains the rest: scribes noticed that 9:12 calls the place lonely, a strange thing to say of a town, and adjusted the wording. The Plain keeps the harder reading.
b: The tension is real: Jesus withdraws to a town, yet the disciples say they are in a lonely spot (9:12). Luke probably means the open country near Bethsaida.

t: "Every day": missing in most Byzantine manuscripts
p: "Every day" is in the oldest manuscripts and the KJV, but not in most later Byzantine manuscripts.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort and the earliest manuscripts; Textus Receptus (KJV "daily")
Most Byzantine manuscripts (the Robinson-Pierpont Byzantine text)

why: The phrase is well attested early and is typical of Luke's style. Scribes probably dropped it to match the same saying in Matthew 16:24 and Mark 8:34. This is one of the places where the KJV, following Erasmus' Greek, agrees with the oldest manuscripts against the Byzantine majority.

p: The oldest manuscripts read "my Son, the Chosen One." Later ones have "my dearly loved Son," as in Mark and Matthew.

readings.w: P45 (200s), P75 (about 175–225), Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus (300s) and others (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Codex Alexandrinus (400s) and the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); Textus Receptus (KJV "my beloved Son")

why: "Dearly loved" is what the voice says in Mark 9:7 and Matthew 17:5, and at the baptism (3:22), so copyists naturally brought Luke into line. "Chosen" is the less expected word, is found in the earliest papyri, and fits Luke, who calls Jesus God's Chosen One again at 23:35.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV name Jesus: "all things which Jesus did."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "which Jesus did")

why: Here a new section began in church reading, so copyists supplied the name, as they often did at the start of a lesson. The past continuous "was doing" fits the scene of many works.

p: The critical text has the present, "is great." The Byzantine text and the KJV have "shall be great."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "the same shall be great")

why: The future tense moves the greatness to the coming kingdom; the present says it is already true. All the critical editions print the present, and a scribe was more likely to change it to the future, which matches other sayings about the last being first (13:30).

a: against you is on your side
p: The oldest text says "against you ... on your side." The Byzantine text and the KJV have "against us ... for us."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
readings.orig: ὃς γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν καθ’ ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐστιν
readings.en: for whoever is not against you is for you
readings.plain: against you is on your side

readings.w: Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "he that is not against us is for us")
readings.orig: ὃς γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν καθ’ ἡμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐστιν
readings.en: for whoever is not against us is for us
readings.plain: against us is on our side

why: Mark 9:40 has "us," and Greek "you" (hymōn) and "us" (hēmōn) differed by one letter and sounded alike in later pronunciation. In Luke, Jesus answers John's "we" with "you," and all the critical editions print it. Mark's own manuscripts are divided the same way (see the variant at Mark 9:40).

p: Many manuscripts, and the KJV, add "as Elijah also did." The oldest do not. 9:54, 9:55 and 9:56 have related additions.

readings.w: P45, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Codex Alexandrinus, Bezae and others, the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "even as Elias did")
readings.orig: καὶ ἀναλῶσαι αὐτούς, ὡς καὶ Ἠλίας ἐποίησεν;
readings.en: and consume them, as Elijah also did?

why: The added words state the allusion to 2 Kings 1:10–12, which every early reader would have caught. If they had stood in the original, no copyist had a reason to remove them; it is easy to see why one would add them as an explanation, in the margin first and then in the text.

t: "You do not know what spirit you are of"
p: The KJV adds Jesus' words: "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of." The oldest manuscripts lack them. 9:56 continues the addition.

readings.w: P45, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and others (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Codex Bezae, some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses, many later manuscripts and the Byzantine text as printed by Robinson and Pierpont; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ εἶπεν, Οὐκ οἴδατε οἵου πνεύματός ἐστε ὑμεῖς·
readings.en: he rebuked them, and said, You do not know what kind of spirit you are of.
readings.plain: rebuked them and said, "You do not know what spirit you belong to."

why: The words are absent from the earliest and most varied witnesses, and those that have them do not agree on how much to add. Metzger judged the words an addition, written in to say what the rebuke contained; some scholars think they may still preserve an old saying. Many readers have loved it, and its thought fits Jesus' teaching (6:27–36), but the evidence shows it was not part of what Luke wrote.

t: "The Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives"
p: The KJV begins 9:56 with "For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them." The oldest manuscripts lack it. Goes with 9:55.

readings.w: P45, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Bezae and others (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses and many later manuscripts; the Byzantine text as printed by Robinson and Pierpont; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ὁ γὰρ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἦλθεν ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων ἀπολέσαι, ἀλλὰ σῶσαι. Καὶ ἐπορεύθησαν
readings.en: For the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them. And they went
readings.plain: "For the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them." So they traveled on

why: This sentence is part of the same expansion as 9:55, and even Codex Bezae, which has the words of 9:55, lacks it. It echoes 19:10 ("the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost") and John 3:17. Its absence from the early witnesses shows it was added to explain why Jesus rebuked the brothers.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "Lord" to the man's offer.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
readings.en: I will follow you wherever you go

readings.w: Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "Lord, I will follow thee")
readings.orig: ἀκολουθήσω σοι ὅπου ἂν ἀπέρχῃ, κύριε
readings.en: I will follow you wherever you go, Lord

why: The next two would-be followers say "Lord" (9:59, 61), and copyists gave the first one the same word. Matthew 8:19 has "Teacher." In the shorter text the first man uses no title at all.

p: The manuscripts are almost evenly divided between seventy and seventy-two, here and in 10:17. The KJV has seventy.

readings.w: P75, Codex Vaticanus, Bezae, some Old Latin, the Old Syriac and Sahidic Coptic, and others (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort; NA28 prints "two" in brackets
Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, the Byzantine majority and others (as reported by Metzger); Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: Both numbers had meaning (see the note), so scribes could have changed either into the other. Seventy was the more familiar symbolic number (the seventy elders, the seventy nations of the Hebrew text), which makes a change from seventy-two to seventy a little more likely than the reverse. The oldest papyrus, P75 (about AD 175–225), reads seventy-two. Metzger, after a detailed study, judged the evidence nearly balanced; the editors of NA28 print "two" in brackets. The Plain follows SBLGNT. 10:17 goes with this verse.

p: The editions differ slightly in the verb. The KJV also reads Capernaum's words differently: "which art exalted to heaven."

readings.w: P45 (200s), Codex Sinaiticus (300s), Alexandrinus (400s) and the Byzantine text (as reported in the NA28 apparatus); SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles
readings.en: you will be brought down to Hades

readings.w: P75 (about 175–225), Codex Vaticanus (300s) and Bezae (400s) (as reported in the NA28 apparatus); NA28, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: you will go down to Hades

why: The meaning hardly changes. "Go down" is the verb of Matthew 11:23 and of the Greek of Isaiah 14:15; scribes may have brought Luke into line with either, or changed "go down" to the stronger "be brought down." P75 and Vaticanus, the strongest early pair, support "go down," which is why NA28 prints it; the Plain follows SBLGNT and the Tyndale House edition, which judge "go down" an assimilation to Matthew and Isaiah.
b: The KJV's "And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted to heaven, shalt be thrust down to hell" follows a Byzantine reading in which the first clause is a statement ("you who were lifted up") instead of a question ("will you be lifted up?"). The question form, in the oldest manuscripts, matches Matthew 11:23.

p: The same division as in 10:1, and the same witnesses on each side.

readings.w: P75, Codex Vaticanus, Bezae and others (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort; NA28 with "two" in brackets
Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, the Byzantine majority and others; Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: See 10:1. The two verses go together.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV have the present "I give"; the critical editions have the perfect "I have given."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "I give unto you")

why: The perfect looks back to the authority already given for the mission (9:1; 10:9, 17); the present makes it a new grant. The meaning differs little.

p: The KJV's "but rather rejoice" follows the Textus Receptus, which adds "rather."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort and the Byzantine text (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
Textus Receptus (KJV "but rather rejoice")

why: Even the Byzantine text lacks "rather." It sharpens the contrast that the Greek "but" already makes. The KJV also has "are written" (the Byzantine ἐγράφη, "were written") for the critical text's perfect "stand written."

p: The oldest manuscripts say Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. The KJV says "Jesus rejoiced in spirit."

readings.w: P75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others (as reported by Metzger); NA28 (with "in" in brackets), SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Codex Alexandrinus and the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "Jesus rejoiced in spirit")

why: The unusual expression "rejoiced in the Holy Spirit" seems to have been simplified by copyists to "in spirit," meaning Jesus' own spirit, perhaps on the model of Mary's "my spirit" (1:47). The longer reading has the better early support and suits Luke's stress on the Spirit (4:1, 14, 18).

t: "And turning to the disciples, he said"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV begin 10:22 with "And he turned to his disciples, and said."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
readings.en: All things were handed over to me

readings.w: Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: Καὶ στραφεὶς πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς εἶπεν, Πάντα μοι παρεδόθη
readings.en: And turning to the disciples he said, All things were handed over to me
readings.plain: Then he turned to the disciples and said, "Everything has been handed over

why: The words were copied from the start of 10:23, probably because a church reading began at 10:22 and needed an introduction. They make 10:22 a private word to the disciples, separating it from the prayer of 10:21.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "when he departed": "on the morrow when he departed."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (the manuscripts on each side are not checked here)
readings.en: and on the next day, taking out

readings.w: Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "when he departed")
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν αὔριον ἐξελθών, ἐκβαλὼν
readings.en: and on the next day, going out, taking out
readings.plain: In the morning, as he left, he

why: The participle "going out" fills in the scene; it changes nothing in the story.

p: The critical text says only that Martha welcomed him. Other editions add "into the house" or "into her house" (KJV).

readings.w: P45 (200s), P75 (about 175–225), Codex Vaticanus (300s) and the Sahidic Coptic (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT
The first hands of Codex Sinaiticus (300s) and C (400s), L and 33 (as reported by Metzger); Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.plain: into the house as her guest

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (400s), Bezae (400s), W (400s) and the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "received him into her house")
readings.orig: ὑπεδέξατο αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτῆς
readings.plain: into her house as her guest

why: The different forms of the phrase suggest that it was added to complete the verb, which needs no object in Greek. The editors are divided; the meaning is the same, since Martha's house is plainly the setting.

t: Jesus' feet or the Lord's feet?
p: SBLGNT and the Tyndale House edition read "Jesus' feet"; NA28 reads "the Lord's feet." The KJV has "Jesus' feet."

readings.w: P45 (200s), P75 (about 175–225), Codex Alexandrinus (400s) and the Byzantine text (as reported in the NA28 apparatus); SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT; Textus Receptus (KJV)
Codex Sinaiticus and the first hand of Vaticanus (300s) (as reported in the NA28 apparatus); NA28, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: at the feet of the Lord

why: Both readings are early. "The Lord" matches Luke's habit as narrator (10:41) and could be original; "Jesus" could also be original and changed to match 10:41. The editors disagree, and the meaning is the same. The Plain follows SBLGNT and the Tyndale House edition. In 10:41 the critical text has "the Lord" and the Byzantine text "Jesus."

a: There is need of only one thing.
t: One thing, or few things or one?
p: One of the best-known variants in Luke. The oldest papyri say "one thing is needed"; other early manuscripts say "few things are needed, or one"; Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts leave the words out, with part of 10:41.

readings.w: P45 (200s), P75 (about 175–225), Codex Alexandrinus (400s) and the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); NA28, Tyndale House GNT; Textus Receptus (KJV "But one thing is needful")
readings.plain: There is need of only one thing.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s) and others (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: ὀλίγων δέ ἐστιν χρεία ἢ ἑνός
readings.en: but few things are needed, or one
readings.plain: Only a few things are needed, or just one.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (400s), which in 10:41 has only "Martha, Martha, you are troubled," and several Old Latin manuscripts, which lack both the worry clause of 10:41 and this clause (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: (omitted; Bezae reads Μάρθα Μάρθα, θορυβάζῃ· Μαριὰμ …)

why: The Plain follows NA28 and the Tyndale House edition against SBLGNT. "One thing" has the two oldest papyri and wide support, and it gives the saying its point: one dish, not many, and the one that matters is Jesus' word. The longer reading may have been made to soften it ("a few dishes will do, or even one"), or it may be original and the shorter a simplification, as Gordon Fee argued. Bezae and the Old Latin witnesses shorten the whole reply, probably to remove a hard saying.
b: Choosing the third reading here removes only the clause in 10:42; Bezae's shorter wording of 10:41 cannot be shown by switching. Many later Christian writers took the "one thing" as the life of prayer and contemplation (see the card on the chapter page).
